content.intro: This lesson focuses on multi-environment deployment. Multi-environment delivery promotes the same tested artifact from development to staging to production using distinct configuration and approval gates. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Multi-Environment Deployment matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Multi-environment delivery promotes the same tested artifact from development to staging to production using distinct configuration and approval gates. Deployment workflows should promote a known artifact through controlled environments, restrict credentials and concurrency, verify health, and define rollback conditions before production use.

content_blocks.caption: Promote the same identified artifact through stages and protect the production boundary.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Multi-environment delivery promotes the same tested artifact from development to staging to production using distinct configuration and approval gates. Deployment workflows should promote a known artifact through controlled environments, restrict credentials and concurrency, verify health, and define rollback conditions before production use. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Development to staging to production
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Environment promotion
items.text: Use a GitHub Environment for deployment-specific secrets, variables, branch restrictions, and reviewer gates. Do not treat an environment name alone as proof that approval rules are configured.

items.title: Reusing the same artifact
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Approval gates between stages
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Preventing accidental production deployments
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - run: echo "Verify known artifact before deploy"
content_blocks.expected_output: The job is associated with the staging environment and read-only repository access; actual deployment credentials and environment protections must be configured separately.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain multi-environment deployment, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Move known build outputs through controlled environments with auditable approvals and recovery plans.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Multi-environment delivery promotes the same tested artifact from development to staging to production using distinct configuration and approval gates. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
